Phase 2 · Security analysis and selection

Select investments the client can actually own

Translate the approved allocation into a focused candidate set, use funds and ETFs as the primary vehicles, and build an intentional portfolio of 8–10 holdings—never more than 10.

Required handoff

Phase 1 is the decision filter

No candidate security or portfolio weight may be approved unless the team identifies the Phase 1 client need, constraint, unresolved question, or downstream guardrail it addresses.

  1. Approved client objective and RRTTLLU constraints
  2. Required and desired return, maximum volatility, and drawdown tripwire
  3. Liquidity dates, cash-flow needs, tax considerations, values, and unique constraints
  4. Committee base and bear macro scenarios with source dates
  5. Phase 1 Analyst Decision Log, including unresolved information gaps and downstream guardrails

Stop before research

If a client guardrail or information gap is missing, return to the Phase 1 decision record. A product search cannot repair an incomplete mandate.

Committee workflow

From guardrail to select/reject decision

1

Translate the mandate

Turn each Phase 1 guardrail and the approved allocation into a measurable screen before researching products. Separate must-pass constraints from preferences.

2

Build a candidate set

Translate the approved allocation and client mandate into a focused candidate set. Funds and ETFs are the primary vehicles; individual securities are limited implementation choices, and individual bonds are not required.

3

Analyze and compare

Use a concise, consistent scorecard for each serious finalist. Compare and reject alternatives briefly; do not complete a full scorecard for every screened name.

4

Challenge the leader

Make a provisional choice first, then use AI to surface the strongest counterargument, missing risk, or contradictory interpretation.

5

Verify and decide

Check every material AI-assisted claim in an approved source, then accept, modify, or reject the provisional choice and record why.

6

Hand off to the portfolio

State the finalist's portfolio purpose, proposed weight, scorecard conclusion, key trade-off, client-fit condition, and the event that would trigger review or removal.

Portfolio boundaries

Build a focused candidate set

Holding count and vehicle mix

Target 8–10 final holdings per client portfolio and never exceed 10. Eight is a valid complete portfolio; do not add a holding merely to fill a slot.

Funds and ETFs are the primary implementation vehicles. Individual securities are permitted only when they add a distinct, mandate-aligned benefit and are limited to two or three total per portfolio. Individual bonds are not required.

  • Every holding has a distinct purpose in the portfolio and fits the approved client mandate.
  • The holding adds useful exposure or diversification without unnecessary duplication or concentration.
  • The position and its underlying exposure have liquidity appropriate to the client and the planned weight.
  • The holding's cost, trading expenses, risks, and implementation demands are proportionate to its benefit.

Consistent final-holding analysis

Use one concise scorecard

Complete this scorecard for each final holding. Do not complete a full scorecard for every screened name.
Exposure and role in the portfolioCost and trading expensesLiquidityHoldings, sector, and style overlapDiversification contributionKey risksClient-mandate fit

Added analysis for an individual security

  • Why an individual security is superior to a fund or ETF for this specific role
  • Idiosyncratic risk
  • Position-size rationale and concentration limit

Rejected alternatives

Compare the strongest realistic alternatives and record why they were rejected in one concise decision record. Full scorecards are required for final holdings, not every screened name.

Instrument-specific analysis

Ask the questions that fit the instrument

Lead: Fixed-Income Analyst

Fixed-income fund, ETF, or limited direct exposure

Does the exposure fit the client's income, capital-preservation, duration, credit, liquidity, tax, and rate-risk guardrails?

Document

  • Fund or ETF objective, benchmark, holdings, cost, liquidity, and income characteristics; use direct-bond terms only if a direct bond is actually proposed
  • Yield or income measure and the return drivers under the base and bear macro cases
  • Duration or interest-rate sensitivity and the effect of a rate move
  • Credit quality, spread, downgrade/default, and concentration risk
  • Overlap, diversification contribution, client fit, proposed portfolio role, and monitoring trigger
  • Concise alternative rejected and the key trade-off

Lead: Equity Analyst

Equity fund or ETF

Does the vehicle deliver the intended equity exposure efficiently without hidden concentration, overlap, trading, liquidity, tax, or style problems?

Document

  • Objective, benchmark or index methodology, style, sector, region, and active or passive approach
  • Top holdings, concentration, sector/style overlap, and diversification contribution
  • Expense ratio, trading expenses, turnover, distributions, and tax considerations
  • Liquidity at both the vehicle and underlying-holdings level
  • Performance or tracking context using comparable periods and current as-of dates
  • Client fit, portfolio role, monitoring trigger, concise rejected alternative, and key trade-off

Lead: Equity Analyst

Limited individual equity

Does this individual security add a mandate-aligned benefit that a fund or ETF cannot provide without creating excessive idiosyncratic or concentration risk?

Document

  • Distinct portfolio purpose and evidence that a fund or ETF is not the better implementation
  • Business and return drivers, valuation context where relevant, and base/bear sensitivity
  • Liquidity, trading expenses, tax considerations, and client fit
  • Idiosyncratic risks and the evidence that makes them material
  • Position-size rationale, concentration limit, diversification effect, and monitoring or exit trigger
  • Concise alternative rejected and the key trade-off

Required inside security analysis

Issuer Reality Check

Decision rule

Yield or recent return alone cannot support a recommendation. The committee must evidence the issuer's financial health, operating outlook, and relevance to the client's mandate.

Complete one concise snapshot for every direct individual security. For a selected fund or ETF, use look-through issuer analysis only when one holding or issuer is material to the exposure, concentration, or risk conclusion; do not create issuer work that duplicates the holding scorecard.

Concise issuer snapshot

  1. Security, issuer, exposure type, portfolio weight, source, and as-of date
  2. Business model and principal revenue drivers
  3. Industry and macro sensitivity under the committee's base and bear cases
  4. Revenue, margin, and cash-flow trend using consistent periods
  5. Liquidity and leverage
  6. Interest coverage and debt-maturity considerations where relevant
  7. One issuer-specific risk and the evidence that makes it material
  8. Conclusion about client fit, allocation implication, and monitoring trigger

Role handoff

Fixed-Income Analyst

Own credit, duration, income, liquidity, and rate-risk evidence for fixed-income funds, ETFs, and any limited direct exposure.

Equity Analyst

Own equity-fund and ETF look-through review and the issuer analysis, idiosyncratic risk, and position-size rationale for any limited individual equity.

Client and Macro Strategist

Explain how the committee's macro scenarios and the issuer's industry sensitivity affect the client-facing thesis and mandate fit.

Portfolio Manager

Apply exposure, overlap, issuer-health, and concentration conclusions to final selection, weight, portfolio trade-offs, and monitoring or exit triggers.

Risk and Derivatives Analyst

Use material issuer and concentration evidence in portfolio-level stress tests and the residual-risk and hedge/no-hedge conclusion.

This is part of the candidate's analysis and selection record, not a separate accounting unit. Keep it concise, cited, and decision-focused.

Required licensed-source research

FactSet Research and Evidence Record

Public/private data boundary

Use your licensed FactSet access to research and download data for your own course work. Submit the final project package and any required licensed-source supporting evidence privately through Canvas. Do not place FactSet captures, exports, credentials, completed proprietary data files, or student work in the public repository.

FactSet layouts, entitlements, and labels can differ. Use course demonstrations and current FactSet support for navigation; this public guide defines the evidence standard, not a click path.

1

Frame the research question

Name the client guardrail, issuer claim, product comparison, or portfolio-risk input the FactSet research must test.

2

Retrieve licensed evidence

Research the relevant security, issuer, credit, financial-statement, fund/ETF, benchmark, holdings, or portfolio-risk data available in your licensed workspace.

3

Record the retrieval

Log what was retrieved, retrieval date, relevant metric or research item, entity/security, as-of period, and source or document reference as appropriate.

4

Interpret

Explain what the evidence means for return drivers, risk, issuer health, product exposure, diversification, or client fit. Do not substitute copied output for analysis.

5

Apply and retain

State how the evidence confirmed, qualified, contradicted, or changed the recommendation, then retain and submit the required licensed-source evidence privately through Canvas under course policy.

Issuer Reality Check

Use current issuer, financial-statement, estimates, industry, ownership, or research evidence as appropriate to evaluate revenue and margin drivers, cash flow, liquidity, leverage, coverage, maturities, outlook, and issuer-specific risk.

Credit and fixed income

Use relevant issue and issuer evidence for price/yield context, maturity and structure, duration or rate sensitivity, credit quality, spreads, liquidity, coverage, debt maturities, and downside risk.

Mutual funds and ETFs

Use relevant product, holdings, benchmark, style, performance, flow, risk, cost, liquidity, and overlap evidence while verifying official product facts in sponsor or filed documents when appropriate.

Corporate issuer analysis

Use consistent financial periods and appropriate issuer evidence to interpret revenue, margins, cash flow, liquidity, leverage, and operating or industry sensitivity.

Portfolio risk inputs

Use appropriately dated risk, return, exposure, correlation, or benchmark inputs and document their definitions, units, limitations, and role in the team calculation.

Five-person ownership

Distinct analysis, integrated selection

Owned work

Client and Macro Strategist

Audit every candidate against the approved client mandate and macro scenarios; reject any security whose rationale depends on an unapproved client fact.

Owned work

Fixed-Income Analyst

Own fixed-income funds and ETFs and any limited direct exposure, including income, yield, duration, credit quality, liquidity, costs, taxes, overlap, and rate-risk fit.

Owned work

Equity Analyst

Own equity funds and ETFs and the limited use of individual equities, including benchmark/style mapping, holdings overlap, fees, trading, liquidity, taxes, idiosyncratic risk, and position size.

Owned work

Portfolio Manager

Integrate analyst finalists, resolve overlap and concentration, set the final 8–10 holdings and weights, and record recommendations rejected and explicit portfolio trade-offs.

Owned work

Risk and Derivatives Analyst

Challenge risk estimates and data comparability, identify residual portfolio risk, and own the evidence for one targeted hedge or a fully supported no-hedge conclusion.

Selection gate

Ready to enter the portfolio?

  • The candidate set translates the approved allocation and client mandate into plausible implementations; the team does not research only its preferred product.
  • Each client portfolio targets 8–10 final holdings and never exceeds 10; eight is complete and no slot is filled without a distinct portfolio purpose.
  • Funds and ETFs are the primary vehicles. Individual securities are limited to two or three total, individual bonds are not required, and any individual security has added rationale, idiosyncratic-risk, and position-size evidence.
  • Every selection names the Phase 1 client guardrail it satisfies and the unresolved fact that could change it.
  • Every final holding has the consistent concise scorecard; alternatives rejected are compared concisely without full analysis of every screened name.
  • The team excludes candidates that duplicate exposure, create unnecessary concentration, lack appropriate liquidity, or fail the client mandate.
  • Return, yield, duration, credit, fee, trading-expense, benchmark, holdings, liquidity, overlap, and performance claims use appropriate approved sources and as-of dates.
  • Every direct individual security has an Issuer Reality Check; fund/ETF look-through is required only when an issuer is material to the exposure, concentration, or risk conclusion.
  • Each recommendation includes a FactSet retrieval record identifying the research retrieved, retrieval date, relevant metrics, source/document reference as appropriate, interpretation, and effect on the decision; licensed evidence is retained according to course policy.
  • The team distinguishes issuer risk, market risk, product risk, and client-suitability risk.
  • Each analyst records recommendations, alternatives rejected, and a key trade-off; a second member reviews the evidence trail.
  • The selected mix is evaluated for overlap and diversification as a portfolio, not only one instrument at a time.

Record the handoff

For every selected candidate, state its portfolio job, proposed weight range, risk contribution, client-fit condition, and monitoring or removal trigger.
